lines.text: The OSI model, explained.
This is Tomi, in Lagos. She takes a photo of her jollof, and taps send.
About one second later, her sister sees it in London, five thousand kilometres away.
In that one second, the photo passes through seven layers. Engineers call it the OSI model.
Let's ride along with the photo.
Layer seven. Application. The trip starts inside Tomi's chat app.
The app says: deliver this photo, to this person.
This is the layer of apps, and the rules they speak, like HTTP for websites, and DNS for finding addresses.
Layer six. Presentation. The photo gets ready for the road.
First it's compressed, so it's smaller. Then it's encrypted, so anyone who grabs it sees only noise.
Layer five. Session. Tomi's phone and the chat server open a conversation, and keep it open while they talk.
Layer four. Transport. The photo is about three hundred kilobytes. Way too big for one trip.
So it gets cut into pieces of fourteen hundred and sixty bytes, and every piece gets a number.
That's TCP. If piece number seven goes missing, TCP asks for it again.
A video call can't wait for that, so it uses UDP instead. Faster, but lost pieces stay lost.
But numbered pieces still don't know where to go.
Quick thing. Want to understand tech like this, a few minutes a day? That is what you get on Teyro.
Okay. Back to the photo.
Layer three. Network. Every piece gets a label with the destination IP address. Like writing the final address on a parcel.
Layer two. Data link. But first, the piece has to reach Tomi's router, a few metres away.
So it gets a second, local label. A MAC address. Like saying, first, take this to the post office down the road.
Layer one. Physical. Now the photo stops being a photo.
It's radio waves across her room. Then voltage in a copper cable. Then flashes of light in glass fibre, on the sea floor, up the coast of West Africa.
Just ones and zeros, crossing the planet.
On the way, routers read the IP label on every piece, and each one picks the next hop. Hop by hop, all the way to London.
Notice what happened. Every layer wrapped the photo in its own label. A parcel, inside a parcel, inside a parcel. That's called encapsulation.
In London, her sister's phone does it all backwards. Light becomes data. Labels come off, one layer at a time. The pieces snap back in order. The photo unlocks. And there's the jollof.
And here's why engineers actually care. When a message doesn't arrive, the layers tell you where to look.
No signal? Layer one. Can't reach your router? Layer two. Router's fine, but nothing beyond it? Layer three. Pieces timing out? Layer four. App error? Way up at seven.
To be fair, the real internet runs on a simpler, four layer model, called TCP/IP. But OSI is still the map every engineer learns first.
Seven layers. Seven jobs. One second. All so a photo of jollof can cross the world.
Want to understand the tech you use every day? Learn it on Teyro.
